adversarial_test_results.prompt: From the middle of the eighteenth century a small number of families kept the lights burning along the northern coast. The work was monotonous and poorly paid, and most keepers stayed only a few seasons before drifting back to the fishing villages they had left behind. Even so, the routine imposed its own discipline. A keeper rose before dawn, trimmed the wick, polished the lenses, and recorded the state of the weather in a ledger that the inspector would later examine. The lighthouse itself stood on a granite ledge that the tide cut off twice a day, and supplies arrived by boat whenever the sea allowed. In winter the spray froze on the iron railing, and the keeper's hands cracked from the cold. The storm surge of 1789 destroyed the outer wall and flooded the oil room, and the service was forced to rebuild the tower on a higher foundation. Historians of the period have argued that the keepers were far less isolated than the romantic accounts suggest. Letters show that they traded tobacco and newspapers with passing crews, and that they often married into the families of pilots and chandlers. The records also reveal a surprising amount of litigation. Keepers sued the board over unpaid wages, and the board sued keepers who abandoned their posts. One celebrated case concerned a keeper who left his station for a single night to bury his wife and was dismissed for neglect. The court held that the dismissal was lawful, though the judges described the penalty as harsh. By the middle of the nineteenth century the introduction of gas, and later of electricity, had begun to make the old skills redundant. The number of keepers fell to a handful, and the lens grinder, once indispensable, found his trade gone; the wick trimmer lost his name to the dictionary. The last of the families moved away in 1912, and the tower passed to the state. Today the building is a museum, and the visitors who climb the spiral stairs see the ledger open at a page from 1801. On that page, in a careful hand, the keeper has recorded a gale, a broken pane, and the arrival of a boat with flour and coal. It is the smallness of the entries that impresses the modern reader: a whole life reduced to weather and supplies, set down each morning before the light was lit. The museum's curator, who has catalogued every page of the surviving ledgers, argues that the keepers wrote for one another rather than for posterity. Their notes on wind direction and cloud cover, she observes, form the longest continuous weather record in the region, and climatologists now quarry the volumes for evidence of old storms. The irony is that the men who kept the record were themselves forgotten, their names surviving only in the margins where they signed for stores.
